summary: Jason Crawford's essay 'Instant stone (just add water!)' argues that cement is a near-magical material. It traces how humans moved from earthen construction to stone-like building, explaining that limestone heated into quicklime and mixed with water and air sets back into rock. The piece covers Roman hydraulic cement, the invention of Portland cement, the compression/tension limits solved by arches and later rebar-reinforced concrete, and modern megaprojects.
one_line: Jason Crawford explains how limestone becomes cement and concrete, from ancient lime and Roman hydraulic cement to Portland cement and reinforced concrete.
key_facts: Humans began settling and building structures about ten thousand years ago.
Earthen construction is limited: dirt is weak, washes away in rain, and works only in hot, dry climates.
Limestone is calcium carbonate (CaCO3), the same substance that makes up seashells.
Heating limestone to about 1,000 °C produces quicklime, removing carbon dioxide to leave calcium oxide.
Mixing quicklime with water releases enough heat to boil the water and produces slaked or hydrated lime, calcium hydroxide.
A lime-water slurry exposed to air sets in a matter of hours by reabsorbing CO2 to return to calcium carbonate, completing the 'lime cycle'.
Cement mixed with water and sand produces mortar; adding gravel or pebbles as aggregate makes concrete.
The Romans added volcanic ash, called pozzalana, to lime to make a hydraulic cement that sets underwater.
Natural cement is a hydraulic cement formed from a mixture of limestone and clay found together in natural deposits.
Since the mid-1800s the most widely used cement has been Portland cement, made by fusing a lime-clay slurry into clinker and grinding it.
Clinker was originally considered waste until grinding it into powder produced a cement stronger than Roman or natural cement.
All cements are strong under compression but weak under tension.
Reinforcing concrete with steel, called rebar, was the new building method of the twentieth century and makes concrete strong under tension too.
Fallingwater, by Frank Lloyd Wright, uses reinforced concrete for cantilevered decks.
The essay describes cement as 'instant stone—just add water!'
